notes.text: That letter is his only tie to this valley in the archive's sources, and it may not be one: "the Santa Clara" may as well be the valley around San Jose, where the drive ended, and no source here places Couts in the Santa Clarita Valley.
notes.claims_absent: any source placing Couts in the Santa Clarita Valley; any tie beyond the 1852 letter
notes.search: \bCouts\b over the whole mirror (26 files); Coutts|Cave J\.|Cave Johnson; Guajome (28 files); Craft: every element's content for 'Couts'
notes.finding: Leon Worden's caption repeated on HS3001 and HS3003 to HS3016 (15 pages; HS3002 does not name him): Couts, "whose presence incidentally was felt in the Santa Clarita Valley at one time or another," "ultimately gave up on his claim" that Guajome was the Ramona home. LW3758 (Leon Worden) sets Couts's Guajome against the del Valles' Camulos, "the 'Home of Ramona' at the west end of the historic Rancho San Francisco (SCV)". Neither gives a date or an act; the caption calls him "Cave Couts Jr." while describing the Tennessee-born father. The sentence "no source here places Couts in the Santa Clarita Valley" is false as written; the narrower claim (no source gives a dated act of his in the valley) holds.
notes.replacement: Jerry Reynolds quotes the letter in his history of this valley, but "the Santa Clara" may as well be the valley around San Jose, where the drive ended.[1] Leon Worden writes that Couts's presence "incidentally was felt in the Santa Clarita Valley at one time or another," without saying when or how; no source here gives a dated act of his in the valley.[n] His Rancho Guajome, in San Diego County, was built about the time the del Valles built at Camulos, and the two later contended to be the "Home of Ramona."[n] (Footnote: Leon Worden, captions to the Lummis "Home of Ramona" pages, HS3001 to HS3016, and to LW3758. The caption names him Cave Couts Jr. but describes the Tennessee-born father; the son was the one who later told the Guajome story, Odell 1939.)

notes.text: Folded into John C. Frémont (#307): no source here names a California Battalion; the sources tell of Frémont's "buckskin battalion", and his record holds it.
notes.claims_absent: any source naming a California Battalion
notes.search: 'california battalion' over the whole mirror; Craft content for 'California Battalion'
notes.finding: 3 mirror files. Dr. Alan Pollack, "Kit Carson, Ned Beale Cross Paths and Alter California's Future" (Heritage Junction Dispatch, Nov.-Dec. 2014): "Fremont's men, now referred to as the California Battalion, met up with U.S. Commodore Robert Stockton in Monterey." Two environmental reports go further and place it here: NorthLake Specific Plan Draft Supplemental EIR (May 2017), section 5.3 Cultural Resources, and Tesoro del Valle Supplemental Draft EIR (Feb. 2018), section 5.5: "Fremont in command of the California Battalion ... Fremont's battalion marched through the Santa Clara River Valley and south to Mission San Fernando." The mirror-grep audit found only Pollack. In Craft, the unsourced WordPress bodies of Edwin Bryant (#313) and the recordDates of Carson (#315) and Pico (#317) also use the name; they are not sources.
notes.replacement: Folded into John C. Frémont (#307). Dr. Alan Pollack writes that Frémont's men were by then "referred to as the California Battalion" when they met Commodore Stockton at Monterey in 1846, and two environmental impact reports in the archive (NorthLake, 2017; Tesoro del Valle, 2018) say the battalion, under Frémont, "marched through the Santa Clara River Valley and south to Mission San Fernando." The battalion's story here is Frémont's march, which his record tells. (Whether the fold stands is Nathan's call; only the stated reason was wrong.)

notes.text: Smythe's 1907 account is the only biography of Couts in the archive. It is an admiring one, and it says nothing of how Couts treated the Native workers whose labor he secured as sub-agent. Wikipedia ... reports that he was tried on several charges, including murder, and acquitted. The archive holds no source for this yet ...
notes.claims_absent: a source on his treatment of Native workers; a source on the trials
notes.search: Couts within 300 characters of murder|acquit|tried|trial|indict|whip|slave; Couts within 250 of buried|cemetery|died|death
notes.finding: Nothing on the trials (survives). But the archive does speak to his use of Native labor: Leon Worden's HS3001-HS3016 caption, "a slaveholder from Tennessee ... used Indian slave labor at his Rancho Guajome (Akins & Bauer 2021:141-142)", and LW3758, "used Indian slave labor (Akins & Bauer 2021:141-142) to build the adobe at Guajome". Odell 1939 (photograph #4743) reports the legend that Helen Hunt Jackson quarrelled with "the young son of the house over his treatment of Indians employed on the ranch". 'Only biography' holds (the NRHP nomination and Odell give sketches, not biographies).
notes.replacement: Smythe's 1907 account is the only biography of Couts in the archive, and an admiring one; it says nothing of how he treated the Native workers whose labor he secured as sub-agent. Leon Worden, citing Akins and Bauer (2021), writes that Couts used Indian slave labor to build the adobe at Rancho Guajome. Wikipedia, used here only as a finding aid, reports that he was tried on several charges, including murder, and acquitted; the archive holds no source for the trials yet.

notes.finding: Leon Worden, "Beale's Cut, parade, the 'Marsha question'," The Signal, June 24, 1998 (article #12334): "Explorers John C. Fremont and Kit Carson rode through the area in the mid-1840s", the area being the pass between the San Fernando and Santa Clarita valleys.
